And the scenarios written by hand from a passage (each checked against it).

scenarios.question: It's 1870. At a friend's house you chatted with someone, but you were never introduced. You pass them in the street the next day. What do you do?
scenarios.answer: Don't bow: without an introduction you aren't acquainted
wrong: Bow, and stop to chat about the party
Raise your hat, but don't stop to speak
Stop and introduce yourself properly
scenarios.note: Persons who have met at the house of a mutual friend, without being introduced, should not bow if they afterwards meet elsewhere. A bow implies acquaintance; and persons who have not been introduced are not acquainted.

scenarios.question: You've been given a letter of introduction to a distinguished family. Do you deliver it in person?
scenarios.answer: Never: it puts you in a most undignified position
wrong: Always: anything else would seem cold
Yes, and wait politely while it's read
Only if the family is expecting you
scenarios.note: Never deliver a letter of introduction in person. It places you in the most undignified position imaginable, and compels you to wait while it is being read, like a servant who has been told to wait for an answer.

scenarios.question: It's winter and you're paying a morning visit. When do you call?
scenarios.answer: Between two and four in the afternoon
wrong: Between nine and eleven in the morning
Between ten o'clock and noon
Any time before luncheon
scenarios.note: A morning visit should be paid between the hours of two and four p.m., in winter, and two and five in summer.

scenarios.question: You're paying a ceremonious call. How long do you stay?
scenarios.answer: No less than ten minutes and no more than fifteen
wrong: About an hour, and not a minute less
At least half an hour, or you'll seem cold
Until the tea things have been cleared
scenarios.note: A ceremonious call should never extend over more than fifteen minutes, and it should not be less than ten minutes.

scenarios.question: You've stood up to leave a call, and your hostess warmly urges you to stay a little longer. What's correct?
scenarios.answer: Go anyway: once you've risen, it's best to leave
wrong: Sit down again: refusing would be ungracious
Stay exactly five minutes more, then go
Stay until the next visitor arrives
scenarios.note: You will, perhaps, be urged to remain, but, having once risen, it is best to go. There is always a certain air of gaucherie in resuming your seat and repeating the ceremony of leave-taking.

scenarios.question: You're paying a call and need to check the time on your pocket watch. What do you do?
scenarios.answer: Ask permission, and apologise, pleading other appointments
wrong: Glance at it discreetly, below the table
Check it openly: callers keep to time
Ask your hostess the time instead
scenarios.note: If you have occasion to look at your watch during a call, ask permission to do so, and apologise for it on the plea of other appointments.

scenarios.question: You're off to a Victorian luncheon party. Do you wear your diamonds and pearls?
scenarios.answer: No: they belong to evening dress, never before dinner
wrong: Yes, but only a single string of pearls
Yes: luncheon is the place to show them off
Only if the hostess is wearing hers
scenarios.note: Diamonds, pearls, rubies, and all transparent precious stones belong to evening dress, and should on no account be worn before dinner.

scenarios.question: You want one gemstone that marks you out as a person of taste. Which does the manual single out?
scenarios.answer: An opal
wrong: A large ruby
A fine emerald
A sapphire
scenarios.note: Of all precious stones, the opal is one of the most lovely and the least common-place. No vulgar man purchases an opal.

scenarios.question: You're choosing a scent for an evening party. Which two does the manual call the most objectionable of all?
scenarios.answer: Musk and patchouli
wrong: Lavender and rosewater
Violet and orange-flower
Sandalwood and bergamot
scenarios.note: Perfumes should be used only in the evening, and then in moderation. Nothing is more vulgar than a coarse ordinary scent; and of all coarse, ordinary scents, the most objectionable are musk and patchouli.

scenarios.question: You're stepping out into the street. What must your gloves be made of?
scenarios.answer: Kid or calf, and nothing else
wrong: Worsted, for warmth in winter
Cotton, for a summer's day
Silk or fine linen
scenarios.note: Never be seen in the street without gloves; and never let your gloves be of any material that is not kid or calf. Worsted or cotton gloves are unutterably vulgar.

scenarios.question: You're a guest at a Victorian dinner and the bread comes round. How do you deal with your piece?
scenarios.answer: Break it: no one cuts bread
wrong: Cut it neatly with your own knife
Slice it with the bread knife provided
Butter the whole piece, then bite
scenarios.note: Then let me tell you that no one cuts bread. You should always break it.

scenarios.question: A roast bird is going round the dinner table. How do you ask for some?
scenarios.answer: Ask for chicken or capon, never 'fowl'
wrong: Ask for 'a little of the fowl'
Ask for 'poultry', the polite word
Point to it and say nothing
scenarios.note: You should have asked for chicken or capon. The word "fowl" is never heard out of the kitchen.

scenarios.question: Your tea is far too hot to drink. What's correct?
scenarios.answer: Wait for it to cool, then drink from the cup
wrong: Pour a little into the saucer to cool
Blow on it gently across the cup
Stir it briskly until it's cool enough
scenarios.note: Nothing can be more vulgar than to pour tea or coffee into a saucer. You should have waited till it cooled, and then have drunk it from the cup.

scenarios.question: You arrive at a dinner party to find dinner already being served. What does one authority advise?
scenarios.answer: Retreat to a restaurant and send an apology
wrong: Slip in quietly and take your seat
Apologise warmly to the hostess and join in
Wait in the hall until the next course
scenarios.note: if you do not reach the house till dinner is served, you had better retire to a restaurateur's, and thence send an apology, and not interrupt the harmony of the courses by awkward excuses and cold acceptance.

scenarios.question: You're laying the table for a Victorian dinner party. How much room does each guest get?
scenarios.answer: Two feet
wrong: Eighteen inches
Thirty inches
Three feet
scenarios.note: A space of two feet should be allowed to each person.

scenarios.question: Two of your dinner guests are celebrated wits. Where do you seat them?
scenarios.answer: Well apart: side by side, they extinguish each other
wrong: Side by side, so they spark off each other
Together at the centre of the table
Both at the head, either side of the host
scenarios.note: It is obviously a bad plan to place two such persons in close proximity. They extinguish each other.

scenarios.question: You're a guest at a Victorian dinner and your host asks whether you'll take "soup or fish". What would an experienced diner do?
scenarios.answer: Take both: they're separate courses
wrong: Choose the soup, as the lighter course
Choose the fish, as the grander course
Leave the choice to your host
scenarios.note: They are as much separate courses as the fish and the meat; and all experienced diners take both.

scenarios.question: The soup has arrived. How do you take it?
scenarios.answer: From the side of the spoon, without a sound
wrong: From the tip of the spoon, in small sips
From the bowl, tipped up to your lips
A whole spoonful at once, tipped in neatly
scenarios.note: In eating soup, remember always to take it from the side of the spoon, and to make no sound in doing so.

scenarios.question: You'd like to offer your neighbour at dinner some mutton. Which word must you never use?
scenarios.answer: "Assist", as in "May I assist you to some?"
wrong: "Send", as in "Shall I send you some?"
"Help", as in "May I help you to some?"
"Offer", as in "May I offer you some?"
scenarios.note: Never offer to "assist" your neighbours to this or that dish. The word is inexpressibly vulgar--all the more vulgar for its affectation of elegance. "Shall I send you some mutton?" or "may I help you to grouse?" is better chosen and better bred.

scenarios.question: Asparagus is served at a Victorian dinner. How do you eat it?
scenarios.answer: Watch what the others do, and follow suit
wrong: Always with a knife and fork, never fingers
Always with your fingers, never cutlery
With a spoon, tips first
scenarios.note: In eating asparagus, it is well to observe what others do, and act accordingly.

scenarios.question: You're eating cherries at dessert. What does the manual prefer you do with the stones?
scenarios.answer: Drop them unseen into your hand, then onto the plate
wrong: Drop them from your lips straight onto the plate
Tuck them into your napkin as you go
Line them up neatly round your plate's rim
scenarios.note: Others cover the lips with the hand, drop them unseen into the palm, and so deposit them on the side of the plate. In our own opinion, the last is the better way

scenarios.question: Someone across the dinner table invites you to take wine with them. What do you do?
scenarios.answer: Pour a little fresh wine, look at them, bow slightly, sip
wrong: Stand and propose a toast to them
Rise and clink glasses across the table
Call out their name and raise your glass high
scenarios.note: In accepting, you have only to pour a little fresh wine into your glass, look at the person who invited you, bow slightly, and take a sip from the glass.

scenarios.question: Your host has lumps of clear ice put into the guests' wine glasses. What does the manual make of it?
scenarios.answer: A new fashion that should be abolished as soon as possible
wrong: A refreshing innovation for the summer
Quite correct, but only with red wines
Acceptable, provided the ice is very clear
scenarios.note: This is an innovation that cannot be too strictly reprehended or too soon abolished.

scenarios.question: You knock over a glass and break it at a dinner party. What's correct?
scenarios.answer: Don't apologise: let your face show your regret
wrong: Apologise at once to the hostess
Offer to pay for a replacement
Send a note of apology the next morning
scenarios.note: If you should unfortunately overturn or break anything, do not apologize for it. You can show your regret in your face, but it is not well-bred to put it into words.

scenarios.question: One slice is left on the dish, and it's offered to you. What do you do?
scenarios.answer: Take it: refusing because it's the last is ill-bred
wrong: Decline it, so as not to seem greedy
Offer to halve it with your neighbour
Leave it for the host
scenarios.note: To abstain from taking the last piece on the dish, or the last glass of wine in the decanter, only because it is the last, is highly ill-bred.

scenarios.question: You're giving a private ball. What should you arrange on the pavement outside?
scenarios.answer: A policeman with a lantern, for the whole evening
wrong: A footman with a torch at each corner
A small band playing on the doorstep
Straw laid in the road to muffle the carriages
scenarios.note: The best thing that the giver of a private ball can do under these circumstances, is to engage a policeman with a lanthorn to attend on the pavement during the evening

scenarios.question: You're hosting a ball. Should you introduce a poor dancer to an excellent one?
scenarios.answer: Never: you'd be punishing one friend to oblige another
wrong: Yes: the good dancer will help them improve
Yes, but only for a quadrille
Only if the good dancer agrees first
scenarios.note: A thoughtful hostess will never introduce a bad dancer to a good one, because she has no right to punish one friend in order to oblige another.

scenarios.question: You and your spouse are at a ball together. Do you dance with each other?
scenarios.answer: No: married people don't dance together in society
wrong: Yes: the first dance is always yours
Yes, but only the last waltz
Yes, but never more than twice
scenarios.note: It is not customary for married persons to dance together in society.

scenarios.question: You're staying at a country house and spot a book in the library you'd like to read in your room. What's correct?
scenarios.answer: Ask to borrow it, and cover it if necessary
wrong: Take it up: a guest has the run of the library
Read it only in the library itself
Take it, and mention it at breakfast
scenarios.note: You should never take a book from the library to your own room without requesting permission to borrow it. When it is lent, you should take every care that it sustains no injury while in your possession, and should cover it, if necessary.

scenarios.question: You're a guest at a country house where they dine late and take no supper. How do you know it's time for bed?
scenarios.answer: A servant appears with wine, water and biscuits
wrong: The host winds the hall clock
The drawing-room lamps are turned down
The hostess rings a little bell
scenarios.note: The signal for retiring to rest is generally given by the appearance of the servant with wine, water, and biscuits, where a late dinner-hour is observed and suppers are not the custom.

scenarios.question: You're talking about an acquaintance who isn't there. What does the manual call the most flagrant offence against taste?
scenarios.answer: Calling them by the first letter of their name
wrong: Calling them "our friend" throughout
Giving their full title every time
Mentioning where they live
scenarios.note: Above all, never name anybody by the first letter of his name. Married people are sometimes guilty of this flagrant offence against taste.

scenarios.question: You're a Victorian gentleman on a call, and you've brought your hat into the drawing-room. You simply must put it down. Where?
scenarios.answer: On the floor
wrong: On a side table
On the lid of the piano
On an empty chair
scenarios.note: The hat, however, must never be laid on a table, piano, or any article of furniture; it should be held gracefully in the hand. If you are compelled to lay it aside, put it on the floor.

scenarios.question: You're a Victorian gentleman sealing a letter. What colour wax do you use?
scenarios.answer: Red, and no other
wrong: Black, as the most sober
Dark blue, as the most refined
Any colour, to suit your taste
scenarios.note: A gentleman should never use sealing-wax of any colour but red, nor paper of any hue but white.

scenarios.question: You're out riding and meet a lady you know who is on foot. You'd like to talk. What's correct?
scenarios.answer: Dismount and lead your horse while you talk
wrong: Stay in the saddle but bring your horse to a walk
Raise your hat and talk from the saddle
Ask her to wait while you stable your horse
scenarios.note: If you are on horseback and wish to converse with a lady who is on foot, you must dismount and lead your horse, so as not to give her the fatigue of looking up to your level.

scenarios.question: You're at an evening party and feeling the cold. Where must you never stand?
scenarios.answer: On the hearth-rug with your back to the fire
wrong: By the window, in the draught
In the doorway
Behind the hostess's chair
scenarios.note: Never stand upon the hearth-rug with your back to the fire, either in a friend's house or your own.

scenarios.question: You're leaving a crowded party. What about saying goodnight to the hostess?
scenarios.answer: Don't seek her out: you might break up the party
wrong: Find her and thank her before you go
Send a servant to give her your thanks
Wait for a lull, then bid her a formal goodnight
scenarios.note: In retiring from a crowded party it is unnecessary that you should seek out the hostess for the purpose of bidding her a formal good night. By doing this you would, perhaps, remind others that it was getting late, and cause the party to break up.

scenarios.question: You've been served at dinner, but the food is far too hot to eat. What's correct?
scenarios.answer: Take up your knife and fork and appear to begin
wrong: Wait until everyone else has been served
Send it back to be cooled a little
Blow gently on each forkful
scenarios.note: As soon as you are helped, begin to eat; or, if the viands are too hot for your palate, take up your knife and fork and appear to begin.

scenarios.question: You're a cavalry officer going to a ball. What must you leave off?
scenarios.answer: Your spurs
wrong: Your sword
Your dress uniform
Your medals
scenarios.note: Cavalry officers should never wear spurs in a ball-room.

scenarios.question: You're a Victorian gentleman dancing a long half-hour with your partner. How much conversation should you manage?
scenarios.answer: At least three or four observations
wrong: None: talking spoils the dance
One remark at the start, then silence
Only a word of thanks at the end
scenarios.note: If it be only upon the news of the day, a gentleman should be able to offer at least three or four observations to his partner in the course of a long half-hour.

scenarios.question: A fellow guest tells an obviously absurd anecdote. What do you do?
scenarios.answer: Listen politely, with every appearance of belief
wrong: Raise an eyebrow, kindly
Gently correct the facts
Ask politely for their source
scenarios.note: No matter how absurd are the anecdotes that may be told in your presence, you must never give any sign of incredulity.

scenarios.question: You're a person of science, and a technical term slips out in polite conversation. What now?
scenarios.answer: Leave it: explaining it would be the greater error
wrong: Explain it at once, in plain words
Apologise, then explain it
Ask whether anyone would like it explained
scenarios.note: If, however, you unconsciously use such a term or phrase, do not then commit the still greater error of explaining its meaning.

scenarios.question: You find an insect in your salad at a dinner party. What do you do?
scenarios.answer: Pass your plate to the waiter without a word
wrong: Quietly mention it to the hostess
Remove it discreetly and carry on
Push the salad aside and leave it
scenarios.note: If in the leaves of your salad, or in a plate of fruit you find a worm or insect, pass your plate to the waiter, without any comment, and he will bring you another.

scenarios.question: At a private dinner you need something from the side table. How do you ask for it?
scenarios.answer: Call a servant by name, or make a sign without speaking
wrong: Call "Waiter!" in a low, pleasant voice
Ask the hostess to have it brought
Fetch it from the side table yourself
scenarios.note: never address those in attendance as "Waiter!" as you would at a hotel or restaurant, but call one of them by name; if you cannot do this, make him a sign without speaking.

scenarios.question: You're cutting fruit at dessert. Which knife do you use?
scenarios.answer: A silver one, never steel
wrong: A steel one, freshly sharpened
Your dinner knife, wiped clean
A small steel blade with a pearl handle
scenarios.note: Do not cut fruit with a steel knife. Use a silver one.

scenarios.question: Dinner is over and you'd love to slip off home. How long must you stay in the drawing-room?
scenarios.answer: At least an hour
wrong: Fifteen minutes is ample
Half an hour at the very most
No time at all: leave after the dessert
scenarios.note: It is excessively rude to leave the house as soon as dinner is over. Respect to your hostess obliges you to stay in the drawing-room at least an hour.

scenarios.question: You're a guest at a Victorian dinner and the cheese arrives. What do you eat it with?
scenarios.answer: A fork
wrong: The tip of your knife
Your fingers, on a piece of bread
A small spoon
scenarios.note: Never put a knife into your mouth, not even with cheese, which should be eaten with a fork.

scenarios.question: You're offered an orange at dessert. What should you peel it with?
scenarios.answer: A spoon
wrong: A small steel knife
Your fingers
A fork
scenarios.note: Apropos of which, I may hint that no epicure ever yet put a knife to an apple, and that an orange should be peeled with a spoon.

scenarios.question: You're a Victorian gentleman at an upstairs window, and a lady you know passes in the street below. Do you bow?
scenarios.answer: No: you may bow up to a window, never down from one
wrong: Yes, a slight bow is quite correct
Only if she looks up and sees you first
Yes, but only after she has bowed to you
scenarios.note: You may bow to a lady who is seated at a window, if you are in the street; but you must not bow from a window to a lady in the street.

scenarios.question: You arrive on a call and see at once that you've come at a bad time, but you've already been seen. What do you do?
scenarios.answer: Don't leave at once: your retreat is cut off
wrong: Apologise and leave immediately
Leave your card and withdraw
Slip out quietly while they're distracted
scenarios.note: do not instantly retire unless you have entered unperceived and can so leave, in which case leave immediately; if, however, you have been seen, your instant retreat is cut off.

scenarios.question: You're having visiting cards printed. What goes on them?
scenarios.answer: Your name and address, and nothing else
wrong: Name, address and profession
Your name and business address
Name, address and your club
scenarios.note: A card should have nothing written upon it, but your name and address. To leave a card with your business address, or the nature of your profession written upon it, shows a shocking ignorance of polite society.

scenarios.question: You're a fashionable Englishman taking a promenade in Hyde Park later in the day. Which gloves?
scenarios.answer: Dark coloured kid gloves
wrong: Reindeer gloves
Chamois-skin gloves
Beaver-skin gloves
scenarios.note: To enter London in his tilbury, beaver skin gloves. Later in the day, to promenade in Hyde Park, colored kid gloves, dark.

scenarios.question: You're a Victorian gentleman who shaves, and money is no object. How many razors should you keep?
scenarios.answer: Seven, one for each day of the week
wrong: Two, used turn and turn about
One good one, well stropped
Three: one each for morning, noon and night
scenarios.note: If you can afford it, you should have a case of seven razors, one for each day of the week, so that no one shall be too much used.

scenarios.question: Lavender gloves have become the new fashion for the evening. Should you wear them?
scenarios.answer: No: they're economical, and all economy is an abomination
wrong: Yes, with a black coat they're perfect
Only at a small, quiet dinner
Yes, if they're fresh each evening
scenarios.note: Recently, indeed, a fashion has sprung up of wearing lavender gloves in the evening. They are economical, and as all economy is an abomination, must be avoided.

scenarios.question: A stranger bows to you in the street, plainly mistaking you for someone else. What do you do?
scenarios.answer: Bow back, to spare them embarrassment
wrong: Stop and explain they've mistaken you
Pretend not to have noticed it
Ask them kindly where you've met
scenarios.note: If any one bows to you in the street, return the bow. It may be an acquaintance whose face you do not immediately recognize, and if it is a stranger who mistakes you for another, your courteous bow will relieve him from the embarrassment arising from his mistake.

scenarios.question: You've sat down to play the piano at a party, but the room is still chattering. What do you do?
scenarios.answer: Begin anyway: don't wait for silence
wrong: Wait on the stool until all is quiet
Strike a firm chord to gain attention
Ask the hostess to call for quiet
scenarios.note: If you play yourself, do not wait for silence in the room before you begin.

scenarios.question: You've been asked to sing at an evening party. How much do you give them?
scenarios.answer: Two verses of a song
wrong: The whole song, every verse
Three songs, then rest
One verse, and a curtsey or bow
scenarios.note: Two verses of a song, or four pages of a piece, are at all times enough to give pleasure. If your audience desire more they will ask for more

scenarios.question: You're writing to the daughters of Mr Smith. How do you address the eldest?
scenarios.answer: As "Miss Smith", the surname alone
wrong: As "Miss Smith Senior"
As "The Elder Miss Smith"
As "Miss A. Smith", with her initial
scenarios.note: Remember, in directing letters to young ladies, the eldest one in a family is addressed by the surname alone, while the others have also the proper name

scenarios.question: You fancy a cigar on your walk. When may you smoke in the street?
scenarios.answer: Only after dark
wrong: Only in the morning
At any hour, if no one is near
Only once you reach the park
scenarios.note: One must never smoke, again, in the streets; that is, in daylight. The deadly crime may be committed, like burglary, after dark, but not before.

scenarios.question: You're paying a call and notice a pile of other people's visiting cards on the table. What's correct?
scenarios.answer: Leave them alone: don't turn them over
wrong: Look through them for mutual friends
Glance at the top few, discreetly
Ask your host about the most notable one
scenarios.note: It is in bad taste, though often done, to turn over the cards on a table, when you are calling.

scenarios.question: You're leaving town and paying your farewell calls. What do you write in the corner of your card?
scenarios.answer: P.P.C.
wrong: R.S.V.P.
N.B.
P.S.
scenarios.note: Leave-taking cards have P.P.C. (pour prendre congé) written in the corner. Some use P.D.A. (pour dire adieu).

scenarios.question: You'd like to give a present to someone well above you in rank. What's always safe?
scenarios.answer: Flowers or game
wrong: Something costly, to show your respect
A fine book, inscribed with their name
Nothing: gifts should only go downwards
scenarios.note: Offerings of flowers and game are unexceptionable, and may be made even to those whose position is superior to that of the giver.

scenarios.question: It's New Year's Day in an old English household. What gift would the ladies be glad of?
scenarios.answer: Pins, or money in their place: hence 'pin-money'
wrong: A china teacup from the master of the house
A silver thimble from each of the servants
A new pair of pattens for the muddy lanes
scenarios.note: Pins were acceptable new year’s gifts to the ladies, instead of the wooden skewers which they used till the end of the fifteenth century. Sometimes they received a composition in money: and hence allowances for their separate use is still denominated “pin-money.”

scenarios.question: It's the eve of Twelfth-day at Pauntley, Gloucestershire, and the farm servants are heading out into a wheat field. What for?
scenarios.answer: To light twelve straw fires and toast the master in cyder
wrong: To bury a cake at the field's edge for the fairies
To walk the furrows ringing handbells at the crows
To sprinkle the young wheat with Christmas ale
scenarios.note: On the eve of Twelfth-day all the servants of every farmer assemble together in one of the fields that has been sown with wheat. At the end of twelve lands, they make twelve fires in a row with straw

scenarios.question: It's Twelfth-night and the plum cake is being sliced. What's hidden inside?
scenarios.answer: A bean for the king and a pea for the queen
wrong: A sprig of holly for the youngest at the table
An acorn for the master and a hazelnut for the mistress
A clove for the cook and a button for the butler
scenarios.note: the cake was full of plums, with a bean in it for the king, and a pea for the queen, so as to determine them by the slices.

scenarios.question: It's Twelfth-day on the Isle of Man, and they're 'cutting off the fiddler's head'. What's going on?
scenarios.answer: He says whom each girl will marry, and it's taken as an oracle
wrong: He plays one last tune and every dancer must freeze
The girls crown him with holly as king of the barn
He must guess which girl is holding the hidden ring
scenarios.note: On Twelfth-day, the fiddler lays his head in some one of the girls’ laps, and a third person asks, who such a maid, or such a maid shall marry, naming the girls then present one after another

scenarios.question: It's the day after Twelfth-day, the first day back at work after Christmas. What do the men get up to in the evening?
scenarios.answer: Setting the women's flax alight, and getting a soaking for it
wrong: Racing their ploughs round the green for a ham
Carrying the yule log's ashes out to the fields
Ringing the church bells backwards to end Christmas
scenarios.note: the burning of the flax and tow belonging to the women, was the men’s diversion in the evening of the first day of labour after the twelve days of Christmas, and that the women repaid the interruption to their industry by sluicing the mischief-makers.

scenarios.question: It's St Agnes' night and you'd like to dream of the one you'll marry. What does old Aubrey say to do?
scenarios.answer: Pull out a row of pins one by one, sticking one in your sleeve
wrong: Walk backwards round the house three times at midnight
Put a slice of wedding cake in your left shoe
Comb your hair before the glass by a single candle
scenarios.note: Upon St. Agnes’ night you take a row of pins, and pull out every one, one after another, saying a Pater Noster, sticking a pin in your sleeve, and you will dream of him or her you shall marry.

scenarios.question: It's Christmas in the West Country and St George and the mummers are at the door. What are they wearing?
scenarios.answer: Shirt-sleeves, beribboned white trousers and tall pasteboard caps
wrong: Masks of straw and coats turned inside out
Sheepskin cloaks and crowns of holly and ivy
Their Sunday best with oak leaves in their hats
scenarios.note: St. George and the other tragic performers are dressed out somewhat in the style of morris-dancers, in their shirt-sleeves, and white trowsers much decorated with ribands and handkerchiefs

scenarios.question: It's 1826 at Hatherleigh in Devon, and you've just come from a funeral. What do the church bells do?
scenarios.answer: Ring a lively peal, as they would elsewhere after a wedding
wrong: Ring the curfew an hour early that night
Stay silent for a month of mourning
Ring muffled at dawn and dusk for a week
scenarios.note: after a funeral the church bells ring a lively peal, as in other places after a wedding

scenarios.question: Our ancestors have moved a church bell to a new steeple. What might it do, unless it's rung in the evening and tied up?
scenarios.answer: Take a nightly trip back to its old church
wrong: Crack at the first christening it rings for
Ring by itself whenever someone in the parish dies
Refuse to sound for the new parson
scenarios.note: When a bell was removed from its original and favourite situation, it was sometimes supposed to take a nightly trip to its old place of residence, unless exercised in the evening, and secured with a chain or rope.

scenarios.question: On St Bartholomew's eve, the boys of St Paul's school run into the scholars of St Anthony's. What do they call them?
scenarios.answer: St Anthony's pigs
wrong: Anthony's owls
Smithfield sheep
Bartlemy babies
scenarios.note: they would call them St. Anthony’s pigs, and they again would call the others pigeons of Paul’s; because many pigeons were bred in Paul’s church, and St. Anthony was always figured with a pig following him.

scenarios.question: It's a great frost, and thousands are flocking onto the frozen Thames. What do they find there?
scenarios.answer: Swings, bookstalls, skittles and dancing in a barge
wrong: A ploughing match on the ice for a silver cup
A tented chapel holding services on the ice
An ice palace built by order of the lord mayor
scenarios.note: Swings, bookstalls, dancing in a barge, suttling-booths, playing at skittles, and almost every appendage of a fair on land, appeared now on the Thames.

scenarios.question: It's Candlemas eve in the Western Isles. The mistress and servants dress up a sheaf of oats and lay it in a basket. What next?
scenarios.answer: Lay a club by it, cry 'Brüd is come!' and read the ashes at dawn
wrong: Carry it three times sunwise round the hearth
Set it on the roof to watch for the first lambs
Burn it at dawn and scatter the ashes on the fields
scenarios.note: lay a wooden club by it, and this they call Brüd’s Bed; and the mistress and servants cry three times, ‘Brüd is come, Brüd is welcome!’ This they do just before going to bed. In the morning they look among the ashes, and if they see the impression of Brüd’s club there, they reckon it a presage of a good crop, and prosperous year

scenarios.question: It's Candlemas at Lyme Regis, and the man who buys the family's wood-ashes has sent his yearly present: a large candle. What's done with it?
scenarios.answer: It's lit at nightfall, and all sit up together till it burns out
wrong: It's set in the window to guide travellers on the road
It's cut in twelve, and one piece burned each month
It's burned on the ash-heap to bless next year's ashes
scenarios.note: The coming of the Candlemas candle was looked forward to by the young ones as an event of some consequence; for, of usage, they had a sort of right to sit up that night, and partake of the refreshment, till all retired to rest, the signal for which was the self-extinction of the Candlemas candle.

scenarios.question: It's St Valentine's eve at Swaffham in Norfolk. Your door flies open and something comes rolling in. What is it?
scenarios.answer: A valentine tied to an apple or orange, then a loud knock
wrong: A wreath of ivy with a sweetheart's initials
A ball of red wool to follow to your valentine
A gingerbread heart with a name iced on it
scenarios.note: Watching for a convenient opportunity, the door is slyly opened, and the valentine, attached to an apple or an orange, is thrown in; a loud rap at the door immediately follows

scenarios.question: It's the night before St Valentine's day and you want to dream of your sweetheart. What goes on your pillow?
scenarios.answer: Five bay leaves: one at each corner and one in the middle
wrong: A sprig of rosemary tied with red thread
A slice of plum cake wrapped in a stocking
Three daisies picked before sunrise
scenarios.note: I got five bay-leaves, and pinned four of them to the four corners of my pillow, and the fifth to the middle; and then, if I dreamt of my sweetheart, Betty said we should be married before the year was out.

scenarios.question: It's St Valentine's day, 1779, in a little Kent village. The girls are crowded round a bonfire, cheering. What's burning?
scenarios.answer: A 'holly boy' figure they've stolen from the boys
wrong: Last year's valentines, for luck in love
A straw figure of Old Winter
The last of the Christmas evergreens
scenarios.note: The girls from five or six to eighteen years old were assembled in a crowd, burning an uncouth effigy which they called a “holly boy,” and which they had stolen from the boys

scenarios.question: It's four in the morning on Shrove Tuesday at Hoddesdon, Hertfordshire, and the old curfew bell rings. What does it mean?
scenarios.answer: Pancakes may be made and eaten until it rings again at eight
wrong: The market may open early for eggs and flour
Every house must sweep its chimney before noon
All fires must be put out until Ash Wednesday
scenarios.note: rang on the morning of Shrove Tuesday at four o’clock, after which hour the inhabitants are at liberty to make and eat _pancakes_, until the bell rings again at eight o’clock at night.

scenarios.question: It's Shrove Tuesday, 1676, and the sun is shining. What do some say that means?
scenarios.answer: The sun will shine as much every day in Lent
wrong: A cold, late spring and a poor hay crop
A wet Easter and plenty of mushrooms
The cuckoo will come early this year
scenarios.note: Others affirm that so much as the sun shineth on that day, the like will shine every day in Lent.

scenarios.question: It's St Piran's day in Cornwall. What are the tinners up to?
scenarios.answer: Taking the day off: the saint told their forebears tin's secrets
wrong: Carrying a block of tin to the church to be blessed
Racing barrows of ore from the pit to the smelting-house
Leaving candles down the mine for the knockers
scenarios.note: having a tradition that some secrets regarding the manufacture of tin was communicated to their ancestors by that saint, they leave the manufacture to shift for itself for that day and keep it as a holiday.

scenarios.question: It's 11 March at Newark-upon-Trent, and the town-hall is giving penny loaves to anyone who asks. Why?
scenarios.answer: For Hercules Clay, who dreamt three times his house would burn
wrong: For the end of a famine the year the Trent froze
For a baker who fed the town through the plague
For a mayor who found the town's charter in a ditch
scenarios.note: Clay (then a tradesman residing in Newark market-place) dreamed three nights successively, that his house was set fire to by the besiegers. Impressed by the repetition of this warning, as he considered it, he quitted his house

scenarios.question: It's mid-Lent in olden times, and boys come into the village carrying a figure made of straw. What happens?
scenarios.answer: It's Death: folk drive them off, or pay to have it taken away
wrong: It's the patron saint: folk bow and give it bread
It's a scarecrow: they set it to guard the sown peas
It's the harvest lord: they ride it round the parish
scenarios.note: On this day boys went about, in ancient times, into the villages with a figure of death made of straw; from whence they were generally driven by the country people; who disliked it as an ominous appearance, while some gave them money to get the mawkin carried off.

scenarios.question: It's Easter Day at Queen's College, Oxford. What's the first dish brought to the table?
scenarios.answer: A red herring set like a man on horseback, on a corn salad
wrong: A pike set like a soldier on guard, on watercress
A great pie baked in the shape of the college gate
A gammon carved like a swan, on a bed of parsley
scenarios.note: the first dish brought to the table on Easter-day, is a red herring, riding away on horseback, that is to say, a herring placed by the cook, something after the likeness of a man on horseback, set on a corn sallad.

scenarios.question: It's Easter eve in Cumberland, and the boys have been begging eggs. What do they do with them?
scenarios.answer: Boil and dye them, then roll and toss them about the fields
wrong: Hide them in the hedges for the girls to find
Leave them on the church step for the poor
Blow them out and hang them on a thorn bush
scenarios.note: These eggs are hardened by boiling, and tinged with the juice of herbs, broom-flowers, &c. The eggs being thus prepared, the boys go out and play with them in the fields; rolling them up and down, like bowls, upon the ground

scenarios.question: It's 1 April 1826, and the youngsters want to make an April fool of you. Which errand might they send you on?
scenarios.answer: To a shop for half a pint of 'pigeon's milk'
wrong: To the grocer's for an ounce of 'sunbeam salt'
To the draper's for a yard of 'thunder ribbon'
To the baker's for a dozen 'yesterday's buns'
scenarios.note: The like knowledge is also gained by an errand to some shop for half a pint of “pigeon’s milk,” or an inquiry at a bookseller’s for the “Life and Adventures of Eve’s Mother.”

scenarios.question: It's 1 April 1825. A boy stops you: 'Sir, there's something out of your pocket.' 'What?' What does he say next?
scenarios.answer: 'Your hand, sir. Ah! you April fool!'
wrong: 'Your watch-chain, sir, and it's gold!'
'A hole, sir, and your money with it!'
'Your handkerchief, sir, waving at me!'
scenarios.note: the waggery of the day is--“Sir, there’s something _out_ of your pocket.” “Where?” “There!” “What?” “Your _hand_, sir--Ah! you April fool!”

scenarios.question: It's Easter Monday at Bury St Edmund's, and there's a spirited game of trap-and-ball going on until sunset. Who's playing?
scenarios.answer: Twelve old women, led by a celebrated 'mistress of the sport'
wrong: The town's twelve aldermen in their gowns
The grammar-school boys against the choir
The bell-ringers against the town's bakers
scenarios.note: On Shrove Tuesday, Easter Monday, and the Whitsuntide festivals, twelve old women side off for a game at trap-and-ball, which is kept up with the greatest spirit and vigour until sunset.

scenarios.question: It's May-day in the London suburbs, about 1805, and a Jack-o'-the-Green is dancing. What's he carrying?
scenarios.answer: A long walking stick with floral wreaths, whisked about
wrong: A tin trumpet to blow at every corner
A brass bell to ring at every door
A wooden sword painted green
scenarios.note: A Jack-o’-the-Green always carried a long walking stick with floral wreaths; he whisked it about in the dance, and afterwards walked with it in high estate like a lord mayor’s footman.

scenarios.question: It's May-day on the green at Temple Sowerby, Westmorland, and there's a grindstone for first prize. What's the contest?
scenarios.answer: Lying: the best liar takes the grindstone
wrong: Wrestling, in the Westmorland style
Carrying a sack of meal up the fell
Whistling longest on a single breath
scenarios.note: which consist of a grindstone as the head prize; a hone or whetstone, for a razor, as the second; and whetstones of an inferior description, for those who can only reach a state of mediocrity in “the noble art of lying.”

scenarios.question: It's dawn on 1 May 1791, and a crowd heads into the fields. What are they up to?
scenarios.answer: Washing their faces in the dew, to make themselves beautiful
wrong: Hunting four-leaved clover to wear all May
Listening for the first cuckoo, for luck
Racing to be first to touch the maypole
scenarios.note: a number of persons went into the fields and bathed their faces with the dew on the grass, under the idea that it would render them beautiful.

scenarios.question: It's 8 May, Flora day, and the whole town is given over to mirth, music and feasting. Someone has been caught working. What happens to them?
scenarios.answer: Carried off astride a pole and made to leap the river, or pay
wrong: Set in the stocks with a garland round their neck
Made to dance alone in the market-place
Their tools hung on the maypole till evening
scenarios.note: Should any persons be found at work, they are instantly seized, set astride on a pole, and jolted away on men’s shoulders, amidst thousands of huzzas, &c., and at last sentenced to leap _over_ the river

scenarios.question: It's Holy Thursday, and the parish schoolboys follow the minister round to the parish boundaries. What are they doing?
scenarios.answer: Striking the boundaries with peeled willow wands
wrong: Lighting lanterns at each boundary stone
Planting an acorn by each boundary stone
Tying a ribbon to each boundary tree
scenarios.note: followed by the boys of the parish school, headed by their master, to go in procession to the different parish boundaries; which boundaries the boys strike with peeled willow wands that they bear in their hands, and this is called “beating the bounds.”

scenarios.question: It's 1751, and a woolcomber and his wife from Weathersfield appear at the manor court of Little Dunmow. What do they claim?
scenarios.answer: The flitch of bacon, by the custom of the manor
wrong: A cheese, for the best-kept cottage garden
A new spinning wheel, from the lord of the manor
The right to graze a cow on the common
scenarios.note: “John Shakeshanks, woolcomber, and Anne his wife, of the parish of Weathersfield, in Essex, appeared at the customary court at Dunmow-parva, and claim’d the bacon according to the custom of that manor.”

scenarios.question: It's Midsummer eve in Ripon, and you moved to a new neighbourhood this year. What does custom expect of you?
scenarios.answer: Spread a table in the street with bread, cheese and ale for all
wrong: Sweep the street from your door to the market cross
Give a loaf to each of the four nearest houses
Ring the minster bell once at midnight
scenarios.note: every housekeeper, who, in the course of the year, has changed his residence into a new neighbourhood, spreads a table before his door in the street, with bread, cheese, and ale, for those who choose to resort to it.

scenarios.question: It's St John's eve in Chester, 1564, and the watch is being set with a pageant 'according to ancient custom'. What's in it?
scenarios.answer: Four giants, a unicorn, a camel, a dragon and hobby-horses
wrong: A whale, a mermaid, a ship and a pair of lions
A castle on wheels, a phoenix and twelve bears
Three kings, a star, an ark and a griffin
scenarios.note: a pageant which is expressly said to be “according to ancient custom,” is ordained to consist of four giants, one unicorn, one dromedary, one camel, one luce, one dragon, and six hobby-horses with other figures.

scenarios.question: It's Midsummer day in a Northumberland village, and there are stools out by the doors. What's on them?
scenarios.answer: Cushions of flowers set in clay, shown to beg for a feast
wrong: Bowls of milk for the passing fairies
Midsummer cakes, one for each traveller
Garlands of St John's wort for the vicar to bless
scenarios.note: it is customary on this day to dress out stools with a cushion of flowers. A layer of clay is placed on the stool, and therein is stuck, with great regularity, an arrangement of all kinds of flowers, so close as to form a beautiful cushion.

scenarios.question: It's the month before Lammas, and the herdsmen's bands are slowly building something. What?
scenarios.answer: Towers of sods with a flagstaff, to meet at on Lammas day
wrong: Bonfires of furze on every hilltop
Stone cairns to mark the summer grazing
A great wicker hut for the Lammas feast
scenarios.note: Each of these communities agreed to build a _tower_ in some conspicuous place, near the centre of their district, which was to serve as the place of their rendezvous on Lammas day. This tower was usually built of sods

scenarios.question: It's 1 August on the Thames, and six young watermen just out of their apprenticeships race from London Bridge to Chelsea. For what?
scenarios.answer: A waterman's coat and silver badge, Dogget's bequest
wrong: A purse of guineas and a new wherry
A gilt cup from the lord mayor
The right to row the king's barge for a year
scenarios.note: to the purchase of a like coat and badge, to be rowed for in honour of the day by six young watermen whose apprenticeships had expired the year before.

scenarios.question: It's Bartholomew-tide in an old printing-house, and the journeymen are making new paper windows. What does the master give them?
scenarios.answer: A feast called a way-goose, before candle-light work begins
wrong: A day's holiday to see Bartholomew Fair
A new leather apron for every journeyman
A shilling each for the ink-maker's ale
scenarios.note: at which time the master printer makes them a feast called a _way-goose_, to which is invited the corrector, founder, smith, ink-maker, &c.

scenarios.question: It's the end of harvest in Hertfordshire, and the reapers tie together the tops of the last blades of corn. What next?
scenarios.answer: Throw their sickles at it; whoever cuts the knot wins
wrong: Race round the field: the first back cuts the knot
Draw straws: the shortest straw cuts the knot
Pelt it with clods: whoever topples it wins
scenarios.note: The reapers tie together the tops of the last blades of corn, which they call “mare,” and standing at some distance, throw their sickles at it, and he who cuts the knot, has the prize, with acclamations and good cheer.

scenarios.question: It's harvest at Hitchin, and a farmer drives furiously home with his last load of corn. What are the people chasing him with?
scenarios.answer: Bowls full of water, to throw on it
wrong: Lanterns, to light him home through the lanes
Handbells, rung till the cart's unloaded
Sheaves of their own, to toss on the load
scenarios.note: it was formerly the custom at Hitchin, in Hertfordshire, for each farmer to drive furiously home with the last load of his corn, while the people ran after him with bowls full of water in order to throw on it

scenarios.question: It's a September play-day at old Eton, and the scholars are off to gather nuts. What must they do first?
scenarios.answer: Write verses on autumn's plenty and the coming winter's cold
wrong: Construe a page of Virgil to the head master
Sing a Latin grace in the chapel
Pay a penny each towards the masters' supper
scenarios.note: but before leave was granted for their excursion, they were required to write verses on the fruitfulness of autumn, and the deadly cold of the coming winter.

scenarios.question: It's autumn in cider country, and the farmers have left plenty of small apples, 'griggles', on the trees. Who are they for?
scenarios.answer: The village boys, who climb up and clear the trees
wrong: The pigs, turned into the orchard after picking
The parson, as part of his tithe
The wassailers, to hang up as offerings at Christmas
scenarios.note: The small apples are called _griggles_. These, the farmers leave pretty abundantly on the trees, with an understanding that the urchins will have mercy on the boughs

scenarios.question: It's bailiff-election day at Kidderminster, and the town-house bell rings. What starts?
scenarios.answer: 'Lawless hour': everyone pelts each other with cabbage stalks
wrong: A race to the church to be first to vote
The town crier reads the old charter aloud
Every shop must put up its shutters for an hour
scenarios.note: On the election of a bailiff the inhabitants assemble in the principal streets to throw cabbage stalks at each other. The town-house bell gives signal for the affray. This is called lawless hour.

scenarios.question: It's Michaelmas day. What's the popular saying about eating goose today?
scenarios.answer: You'll never want money all the year round
wrong: Your own geese will thrive all year
You'll be wed before Christmas
The frost will hold off till Martinmas
scenarios.note: If you eat goose on Michaelmas-day you will never want money all the year round.

scenarios.question: It's the first week of October at St Magnus, London Bridge. By Sir John Salter's will, what must the Salters' beadles say there?
scenarios.answer: 'How do you do brother Salter? I hope you are well!'
wrong: 'God rest Sir John, who gave us bread and salt!'
'Brother Salter, the salt is sweet this year!'
'Here's to Sir John, the Salters' good friend!'
scenarios.note: ordered that the beadles and servants should go to the said church the first week in October, three times each person, and say, “How do you do brother Salter? I hope you are well!”

scenarios.question: It's St Simon and St Jude's day. What weather does everyone expect?
scenarios.answer: Rain: the day is held as rainy as St Swithin's
wrong: The first hard frost of the winter
A gale to strip the last leaves
A fine day, the last of the summer
scenarios.note: This anniversary was deemed as rainy as St. Swithin’s.

scenarios.question: It's Hallowe'en in Ireland. A young woman lays three nuts on the bars of the grate, each named for a lover. One cracks and jumps. What does it mean?
scenarios.answer: That lover will prove unfaithful
wrong: That lover will propose before Christmas
That lover is thinking of her that very moment
That lover will travel far before they meet
scenarios.note: If a nut cracks or jumps, the lover will prove unfaithful; if it begins to blaze or burn, he has a regard for the person making the trial.

scenarios.question: It's the eve of 1 November in North Wales, and the autumn fire is lit. Everyone runs through the smoke and throws in a stone. Why do they all run off at the end?
scenarios.answer: To escape the black short-tailed sow
wrong: To chase the last sparks down the hill
To be home before the church bell tolls
To beat the fairies to the crossroads
scenarios.note: such as running through the fire and smoke, each casting a stone into the fire, and all running off at the conclusion to escape from the black short-tailed sow

scenarios.question: At the country sports, ten or eleven candidates are tied in something up to their necks for a race of about five hundred yards. What's the sport?
scenarios.answer: Jumping in sacks, for a cheese
wrong: Rolling in barrels, for a ham
Hopping in hampers, for a goose
Shuffling in blankets, for a pudding
scenarios.note: Ten or eleven candidates are chosen; they are tied in sacks up to their necks, and have to jump about five hundred yards.

scenarios.question: Martins have built a nest in the corner of your bedroom window. What does it mean?
scenarios.answer: Good luck, the more so if the same birds come back
wrong: A wedding in the house within the year
A hard winter is on its way
Someone in the house will soon go overseas
scenarios.note: It is considered a presage of good, for this bird to build its nest in the corner of the bedroom-window; and particularly so, should the first inhabitants return in the season.

scenarios.question: It's St Clement's day and the boys have been round the houses. What have they collected, and what happens to it?
scenarios.answer: Apples, roasted together, some dropped hot into ale or cider
wrong: Candle-ends, to light a bonfire on the green
Flour and lard, for a great pancake on the hill
Nuts, cracked by the fire to tell fortunes
scenarios.note: Having collected a good store of apples, which they seldom failed to do, the boys repaired to some one of their houses, where they roasted and ate the apples

scenarios.question: It's early December in the north of England, and there's a Penny Lottery on. What might your penny win you?
scenarios.answer: A whole garden, sold while it lies dormant
wrong: A fat goose for Christmas
A year's free shaving at the barber's
A new Sunday coat
scenarios.note: About this time, when gardens look in a dormant state, there are frequently Penny Lotteries in the north of England; and very often a whole garden is purchased for one penny.

scenarios.question: It's St Nicholas's day, long ago, and the choir boys of a cathedral choose one of their number. To be what?
scenarios.answer: A bishop, in robes and mitre, until Innocents' day
wrong: The saint's page, carrying gifts to the poor
Keeper of the keys, to lock the masters out
Captain of the bell-ringers until New Year
scenarios.note: the choir boys in cathedral churches, chose one of their number to maintain the state and authority of a bishop, for which purpose the boy was habited in rich episcopal robes, wore a mitre on his head, and bore a crosier in his hand

scenarios.question: It's the St Nicholas visit. Each of the family leaves a shoe on a table in a room that's then carefully locked. What's found in the morning?
scenarios.answer: The table covered with bonbons, toys and trinkets
wrong: Every shoe newly blacked and mended
A letter from the saint tucked in each shoe
Each shoe turned round to point at the door
scenarios.note: the board is found covered with _bons bons_, toys, and trinkets.

scenarios.question: It's St Thomas's day in Kent, and women are going 'a gooding' for money. What do they give in return?
scenarios.answer: Sprigs of palm and branches of primroses
wrong: Spiced cakes baked that morning
Sprigs of holly and mistletoe
Candles dipped for the long nights
scenarios.note: Going a _gooding_ on St. Thomas’s day formerly prevailed in England. Women begged money, and in return presented the donors with sprigs of palm and branches of primroses.

scenarios.question: It's Christmas eve, 1790, in Devon, and the country people sing a wassail. What do they do with the toast from the wassail-bowl?
scenarios.answer: Throw it to the apple-trees, for a fruitful year
wrong: Float it on the mill-pond for the fish
Lay it on the hearth for the Christmas spirits
Share it with the first stranger at the door
scenarios.note: it was then customary for the country people to sing a wassail or drinking-song, and throw the toast from the wassail-bowl to the apple-trees in order to have a fruitful year.

scenarios.question: Christmas eve at Quainton, Bucks: two thousand people go by lantern-light to watch a blackthorn bud. It doesn't. What do they decide?
scenarios.answer: That 25 December can't be the right Christmas-day
wrong: That the parish must plant a new thorn
That a poor harvest is coming next year
That the vicar must bless the tree at Twelfth-night
scenarios.note: The people finding no appearance of a bud, it was agreed by all, that December 25 (new style) could not be the right Christmas-day, and accordingly refused going to church

scenarios.question: It's Christmas morning, and the old folk tell the children to go down to the valley and stoop to the ground. What will they hear?
scenarios.answer: The bells of a church beneath them, ringing merrily
wrong: The fairies' Christmas feast under the hill
The old mill turning beneath the water
The river singing under the ice
scenarios.note: Even now, it is usual on Christmas morning for old men and women to tell their children and young friends to go to the valley, stoop down, and hear the bells ring merrily.

scenarios.question: It's St Stephen's day in the North Riding of Yorkshire. Large goose pies go to needy neighbours, all but one. What becomes of that one?
scenarios.answer: It's put by and not tasted till Candlemas
wrong: It's given to the vicar for Twelfth-night
It's sent to the lord of the manor with the rent
It's eaten by the bell-ringers on New Year's eve
scenarios.note: except one which is carefully laid up, and not tasted till the purification of the virgin, called Candlemas.

scenarios.question: It's Childermas, 1517, among the sages of the law, and Henry VIII has ordered that a mock king should sit and have due service. Which king?
scenarios.answer: The king of cockneys
wrong: The king of the quill
The king of the apprentices
The king of the woolsack
scenarios.note: “that the _king of cockneys_, on _Childermas-day_, should sit and have due service; and that he and all his officers should use honest manner and good order

scenarios.question: It's St Patrick's day: the bells are ringing and the piper's playing. What have the children got pinned to their sleeves?
scenarios.answer: 'Patrick's crosses': little prints of a cross or the saint
wrong: Tiny paper stars cut out by their mothers
Paper harps painted gold
Little bells to ring in the procession
scenarios.note: children have “Patrick’s crosses” pinned to their sleeves. These are small prints of various kinds; some of them merely represent a cross, others are representations of Saint Patrick

scenarios.question: It's the king's birthday, 1819, at Bexhill in Sussex, and twenty-five old men dine together at the Bell Inn. What's special about them?
scenarios.answer: Their ages averaged eighty-one, the king's own age
wrong: Each had served at sea under Nelson
They were all born the same week as the king
They had rung the bells at his coronation
scenarios.note: Twenty-five old men, inhabitants of the parish, whose united ages amounted to 2025, averaging eighty-one each (the age of the king) dined together at the Bell Inn

scenarios.question: You're hanging a horseshoe over the door as a luck token. Which way up should it go, by the popular notion?
scenarios.answer: Points upward, or else the luck may be spilled out
wrong: Points towards the street, to call the luck in
On its side, with the points towards the hinges
Points to the left, towards the rising sun
scenarios.note: From a scientific standpoint, therefore, the horse-shoe, when used as a protective symbol, should be placed with its convex arch uppermost; but as a luck token, the reverse position is the proper one, else, according to a popular notion, the luck may be spilled out.

scenarios.question: You're nailing up a horseshoe in eastern Pennsylvania. Which way do the prongs point, and why?
scenarios.answer: Inward, so the luck may be spilled into the house
wrong: Outward, to catch the luck of passers-by
Downward, so the luck runs onto the doorstep
Towards the chimney, where luck comes in
scenarios.note: In eastern Pennsylvania, however, even in recent times, the horse-shoe is often placed with the prongs pointing inward, so that the luck may be spilled into the house.

scenarios.question: You find a horseshoe in Northumberland and carefully count the holes with no nails in. What do they tell you?
scenarios.answer: How soon you may expect to be married
wrong: How many children you will one day have
How many pounds you will come into this year
How many visitors will call before Sunday
scenarios.note: In Northumberland the holes free of nails are carefully counted, as these indicate, presumably in years, how soon the finder of the shoe may expect to be married.

scenarios.question: You live among the Wends of the Spreewald and have just found a horseshoe. What mustn't you do?
scenarios.answer: Tell any neighbour about your good fortune
wrong: Pick it up with your bare right hand
Carry it home after the sun has set
Let it touch the ground a second time
scenarios.note: the lucky finder of a horse-shoe is careful not to tell any neighbor of his good fortune, but proceeds at once to fasten the shoe over the door of his house, or on the threshold, with three nails, and by three blows of a hammer, so that evil spirits may not enter.

scenarios.question: You find a horseshoe in Tuscany. Where do you keep it?
scenarios.answer: In a little red bag with some hay, in your bed
wrong: In a blue bag hung over the kitchen fire
Under the doorstep, wrapped in a vine leaf
In your left boot until the next full moon
scenarios.note: In Tuscany a horse-shoe when found is placed in a small red bag with some hay, which the Tuscans consider also a luck-bringing article, and the twofold charm is kept in its owner’s bed.

scenarios.question: In the Thuringian Forest, an old shoe off the road won't do for your bedroom threshold. Who must have forged it?
scenarios.answer: A bachelor of good character, on Saint John's Eve
wrong: A seventh son, on Midsummer morning
A widowed smith, at the dark of the moon
A smith's apprentice, on his very first day
scenarios.note: in order to serve its purpose as a talisman, a Thuringian horse-shoe must have been forged by a bachelor of wholesome life and good character, on Saint John’s Eve.

scenarios.question: It's about 1850 in Perthshire, and your minister preaches against the horseshoes on the farm doors. What does the parish do?
scenarios.answer: Move them from the outsides of the doors to the insides
wrong: Paint them black so he can't spot them
Nail them up on the church door instead
Bury them under the doorsteps
scenarios.note: his superstitious parishioners removed the guardian horse-shoes from the outsides of the doors, and nailed them up on the insides.

scenarios.question: In the far north of Scotland, you and your neighbour have fallen out. Where does a horseshoe keep you both safe?
scenarios.answer: Placed between your two houses
wrong: Over your door, points towards their house
Buried at midnight under their gate
On your roof, facing their chimney
scenarios.note: if a horse-shoe be placed between the houses of quarrelsome neighbors, neither incurs any risk of evil as a result of the other’s ill-wishes.

scenarios.question: You're out with the Scottish fishing fleet and a shipmate swears. What does everyone do?
scenarios.answer: Cry "Cauld airn!" and each grab a piece of iron
wrong: Spit over the side and touch the mast
Throw a pinch of salt into the sea
Turn round three times and whistle
scenarios.note: if, when plying their vocation, one of their number chance to indulge in profanity, the others at once call out, “Cauld airn!” and each grasps a handy piece of the metal as a counter influence to the misfortune which would else pursue them throughout the day.

scenarios.question: You walk into a house in north-west Scotland while the butter is being churned. What's expected of you?
scenarios.answer: Lay your hand on the churn, to show you mean no harm
wrong: Leave at once and come back when it's done
Drop a pinch of salt in for luck
Say "God speed the butter" from the doorway
scenarios.note: In northwestern Scotland whoever enters a house where butter is being made is expected to lay his hand upon the churn, thereby signifying that he has no evil designs against the butter-maker

scenarios.question: It's 1627, and the salt falls towards a superstitious guest at dinner. What finally comforts him?
scenarios.answer: A waiter pouring wine in his lap
wrong: Throwing a pinch over his left shoulder
Being served a second helping of bread
The whole table drinking his health
scenarios.note: Bishop Hall wrote, in 1627, that when salt fell towards a superstitious guest at dinner, he was wont to exhibit signs of mental agitation, and refused to be comforted until one of the waiters had poured wine in his lap.

scenarios.question: You spill the salt in Norway. What will it cost you, by popular belief?
scenarios.answer: As many tears as it takes to dissolve the salt
wrong: A year of bad luck for every grain
A lost coin for every grain
Seven days without a letter
scenarios.note: According to a popular Norwegian belief, one will shed as many tears as may suffice to dissolve the quantity of salt which he has spilled

scenarios.question: You spill salt in Bucks County, Pennsylvania. Besides tossing a pinch over your left shoulder, what must you do?
scenarios.answer: Crawl under the table and come out the other side
wrong: Walk three times round the table
Sweep it up with your left hand only
Move your chair to the other side
scenarios.note: In Bucks County, Pennsylvania, in order to avert ill-luck after salt has been spilled, one should not only toss a pinch of the spilled salt over the left shoulder, but should also crawl under a table and come out on the opposite side.

scenarios.question: You've spilt salt in New England, and a toss over the left shoulder isn't enough. Where must the grains go?
scenarios.answer: On the stove
wrong: Out of the front door
Down the well
Under your pillow
scenarios.note: for in order thoroughly to break the spell, these particles must be thrown on the stove.

scenarios.question: By one remarkable superstition, what awaits you in the hereafter for spilling salt?
scenarios.answer: A year outside the gate of Paradise for every grain
wrong: Counting every grain again before you go in
No salt at all at the heavenly feast
A year sweeping heaven's steps for every grain
scenarios.note: as a penalty for spilling salt, one must wait outside the gate of Paradise for as many years as there are grains of salt spilled.

scenarios.question: A 1586 book of symbols says spilling salt on the table is ominous. What is lucky to spill?
scenarios.answer: Wine, especially if unmixed with water
wrong: Milk, especially fresh from the cow
Water, especially from a holy well
Oil, especially the first pressing
scenarios.note: Wherefore many consider it ominous to spill salt on the table, and, on the other hand, propitious to spill wine, especially if unmixed with water.

scenarios.question: In the north of England, someone helps you to salt at table. What does the old couplet say?
scenarios.answer: "Help me to salt, help me to sorrow"
wrong: "Pass the salt, pass the luck"
"Salt from a friend, friendship's end"
"Salt in hand, trouble on land"
scenarios.note: it is reckoned unlucky to be helped to salt at table, and this idea has found expression in the popular couplet, “Help me to salt, help me to sorrow.”

scenarios.question: In Russia, you have to pass your neighbour the salt. How do you stop it causing a quarrel?
scenarios.answer: Smile amicably as you offer it
wrong: Pass it with your left hand
Set it down rather than hand it over
Say a blessing over it first
scenarios.note: But if in proffering the salt one smiles amicably, all danger of a quarrel is happily averted, and the act is wholly relieved of its ominous character.

scenarios.question: You run a Japanese household. When won't you buy salt?
scenarios.answer: At night
wrong: On the first day of the month
When it's raining
On your own birthday
scenarios.note: The mistress of a household will not buy it at night, and when purchased in the daytime a small quantity is thrown into the fire in order to prevent discord in the family, and to avert misfortune generally.

scenarios.question: It's 1789 and Robert Burns's family escort him to his new house at Ellisland. What's carried in their midst?
scenarios.answer: A bowl of salt resting on the family Bible
wrong: A horseshoe on a velvet cushion
A loaf of bread and a lump of coal
Embers from the old hearth in an iron pot
scenarios.note: he was escorted on his route thither along the banks of the river Nith by a procession of relatives, and in their midst was borne a bowl of salt resting on the family Bible.

scenarios.question: Why might a Scottish fisherman throw a little salt into the sea?
scenarios.answer: To blind the fairies
wrong: To calm the waves
To pay the sea for its fish
To keep the nets from rotting
scenarios.note: Scotch fishermen have a traditional custom of salting their nets “for luck,” and they also sometimes throw a little salt into the sea “to blind the fairies.”

scenarios.question: You're an Andalusian peasant. What's the most endearing thing you can call your sweetheart?
scenarios.answer: "The salt-box of my love"
wrong: "The sugar-bowl of my heart"
"The honey-pot of my days"
"The bread-bin of my soul"
scenarios.note: no more endearing or flattering language can be used in addressing a woman, whether wife or sweetheart, than to call her “the salt-box of my love.”

scenarios.question: It's St Augustine's time, and you sneeze while putting on your shoes in the morning. What do you do?
scenarios.answer: Go back to bed
wrong: Take them off and start with the other foot
Stay indoors until noon
Put the shoes on the wrong feet
scenarios.note: St. Augustine wrote that, in his time, so prevalent was faith in the omens of sneezing that a man would return to bed if he happened to sneeze while putting on his shoes in the morning.

scenarios.question: In Elizabethan England, you sneeze twice while talking business with someone. What should you do?
scenarios.answer: Get up and go straight about your business: you'll prosper
wrong: Let the matter drop, for it will come to nought
Wait for a third sneeze before deciding
Shake hands at once and seal the bargain
scenarios.note: If that any man talk with another about any matter and snese twise or iiij tymes, let him by and by arise, yf he sett, or yf he be stand, let him move hymself and go straightway without any stays about his business, for he shall prosper.

scenarios.question: In Selkirkshire, you sneeze as you first step out of bed. What does it tell you?
scenarios.answer: Strangers will come today, one for each sneeze
wrong: Letters will come today, one for each sneeze
Rain will fall today, an hour for each sneeze
You'll quarrel today, once for each sneeze
scenarios.note: “When they sneeze in first stepping out of bed in the morning, they are thence certified that strangers will be there in the course of the day, in numbers corresponding to the times they sneeze.”

scenarios.question: In old Flanders, someone sneezes while you're in the middle of a story. What does it prove?
scenarios.answer: That what you're saying is the truth
wrong: That you'd better change the subject
That a stranger is at the door
That you'll be proved wrong by nightfall
scenarios.note: It was a Flemish belief that a sneeze during a conversation proved that what one said was the truth, a doctrine which must have commended itself to snuff-takers.

scenarios.question: You sneeze twice in old Japan. What does it mean?
scenarios.answer: Someone is finding fault with you
wrong: Someone is praising you
You've simply caught a cold
An old friend is about to visit
scenarios.note: Thus, one sneeze indicates that some one is praising him, while two betoken censure or disparagement; a triple sneeze is commonplace, and means simply that a person has taken cold.

scenarios.question: You sneeze on New Year's Eve in China, an ill omen for the year. How do you put it right?
scenarios.answer: Beg a tortoise cake from each of three families, eaten by midnight
wrong: Light three red candles before midnight
Sweep the doorstep three times before midnight
Eat a bowl of noodles without speaking
scenarios.note: According to a Chinese superstition a sneeze on New Year’s Eve is ominous for the coming year; and, to offset this, the sneezer must visit three families of different surnames, and beg from each a small tortoise-shaped cake, which must be eaten before midnight.

scenarios.question: You're a gentleman in old France and you sneeze in company. What does etiquette require?
scenarios.answer: Take off your hat, then return everyone's salutes
wrong: Turn your back and cover your face
Bow to the host and beg his pardon
Leave the room until it has passed
scenarios.note: In France the rules of etiquette formerly required that a gentleman who sneezed in the presence of another should take off his hat, and on the subsidence of the paroxysm he was expected formally to return the salutes of all present.

scenarios.question: Someone sneezes on Rarotonga. What do you say, and why?
scenarios.answer: "Ha! you have come back!", to welcome their wandering spirit
wrong: "Go away!", to chase a spirit out of them
"Stay a while!", to keep their luck from leaving
"Bless the wind!", for the breath that left them
scenarios.note: They therefore deem it proper to welcome back the wandering spirit, the form of greeting varying in the different islands. The phrase employed by the natives of Raratonga, for example, means “Ha! you have come back!”

scenarios.question: You sneeze in Siam. By the Siamese account, what has just happened?
scenarios.answer: The Supreme Judge has turned to your page in his book
wrong: Someone in the house is about to quarrel
Your luck has turned for the coming week
A traveller has set out on the road to you
scenarios.note: They believe that the Supreme Judge of the spiritual world is continually turning over the pages of a book containing an account of the life and doings of every human being; and when he comes to the page relating to any individual, the latter never fails to sneeze.

scenarios.question: A poor soul under a Wurmlingen bridge sneezes three times as you cross. What would have freed him?
scenarios.answer: Saying "God help thee!" for the third sneeze too
wrong: Dropping a coin into the stream below
Calling his name out loud three times
Crossing the bridge again backwards
scenarios.note: Thereupon a voice from under the bridge exclaimed pitifully, “If you had only said, ‘God help thee!’ a third time, I should have been freed from the spell which binds me.”

scenarios.question: Someone hiccups in Turkistan. What's the polite, luck-bringing thing to say?
scenarios.answer: "You stole something from me"
wrong: "Someone is missing you"
"Your soul is in a hurry"
"Somebody is telling tales"
scenarios.note: When, also, any one hiccoughs, it is etiquette to say, “You stole something from me,” and this phrase at such times is supposed to produce good luck.

scenarios.question: It's 1455 in Germany and you sneeze three times. What did popular belief say that meant?
scenarios.answer: Four thieves are about the house
wrong: Three guests are on the road
A letter is coming from far away
Rain before the next church bell
scenarios.note: we learn that in Germany there was a popular belief that three sneezes indicated the presence of four thieves around the house.

scenarios.question: Your cat sneezes in Shetland. What's it telling you?
scenarios.answer: Cold north winds in summer, snow in winter
wrong: A visitor before the week is out
A good catch for the boats tomorrow
A letter from someone over the sea
scenarios.note: In Shetlandic and Welsh folk-lore the sneeze of a cat indicates cold north winds in summer and snow in winter

scenarios.question: You farm by Hesiod's "Works and Days". Which day of the month is excellent for reaping corn?
scenarios.answer: The eleventh
wrong: The seventh
The first
The fifteenth
scenarios.note: Thus he recommends the eleventh of the month as excellent for reaping corn, and the twelfth for shearing sheep.

scenarios.question: Why won't West Sussex folk let the children go blackberrying on 10 October?
scenarios.answer: The Devil goes afield that day
wrong: The fairies claim the hedges that day
The first frost spoils the fruit that day
The berries belong to the birds from then
scenarios.note: The peasantry of West Sussex in England will not permit their children to go blackberrying on the tenth day of October, on account of a belief that the Devil goes afield on that day

scenarios.question: You're getting married in 1890s Glasgow, like a large share of couples there. Which day do you pick?
scenarios.answer: Friday
wrong: Saturday
Wednesday
Monday
scenarios.note: This opinion finds favor in Glasgow, where a large proportion of marriages take place on this day; whereas, in the midland counties of England, less than two per cent. of the weddings occur on the sixth day of the week.

scenarios.question: In Shropshire, you hear something new on a Friday. What does it do to you?
scenarios.answer: Gives you another wrinkle and adds a year to your age
wrong: Brings a week of rain after it
Turns out to be false by Sunday
Means worse news before the month is out
scenarios.note: according to a Shropshire saying, “if you hear anything new on a Friday, it gives you another wrinkle on your face, and adds another year to your age.”

scenarios.question: It's a Friday in Ireland and a stranger knocks. What should you take especial care to do?
scenarios.answer: Not open the door to them
wrong: Offer them a cup of milk
Ask their name before they cross the threshold
Give them a pinch of salt as they leave
scenarios.note: In Ireland Friday is _facile princeps_ among unlucky days, and especial care should be taken not to open the door of one’s dwelling to any stranger on that day.

scenarios.question: Paris theatres put on nearly two hundred new pieces a year. For many years, how many opened on a Friday?
scenarios.answer: Not one
wrong: About one in seven
Only the comedies
Only the tragedies
scenarios.note: This is shown by statistics of the Parisian theatres, where there are produced on an average nearly two hundred new pieces annually, and for many years not one of these has had its first performance on a Friday.

scenarios.question: You're giving a Paris dinner party and find you're thirteen. Who do you send for?
scenarios.answer: A quatorzième, to occupy the fourteenth seat
wrong: A priest, to bless the table
A footman, to lay one place fewer
The concierge's cat, for the fourteenth chair
scenarios.note: The Parisian _pique-assiette_, a person whose title corresponds to the English “trencher friend” or “sponger,” is also known as a _quatorzième_, his chief mission being to occupy the fourteenth seat at a banquet.

scenarios.question: You've rashly dined thirteen at table. How is all the evil averted?
scenarios.answer: The whole company rises to its feet together
wrong: The youngest guest sits apart for the pudding
A fourteenth place is laid for the pudding
Everyone touches the table leg at once
scenarios.note: All evil, however, was supposed to be averted by the entire company rising to their feet together.

scenarios.question: You've booked the thirteenth box at an Italian theatre. What number is on its door?
wrong: 12bis
XIII
