scenarios.note: In Italy shrewd theatrical managers have found it expedient to change the number of Box 13 to 12A

scenarios.question: You're in Persia and need to mention the number thirteen. What do you say instead?
scenarios.answer: "Much more", or "nothing"
wrong: "Twelve and one"
"A baker's dozen"
"The number after twelve"
scenarios.note: When they wish to allude to this number, instead of mentioning the proper term, they use words meaning “much more” or “nothing.”

scenarios.question: Your baker gives you thirteen loaves for twelve. Why did the custom begin?
scenarios.answer: Heavy fines for short weight: the extra loaf was a precaution
wrong: The oven held twelve loaves and one for the baker
The thirteenth was a tithe loaf for the church
Bakers kept one back to test the batch
scenarios.note: it was formerly a common practice to give thirteen loaves for twelve, the extra piece being called the _in-bread_ or _to-bread_. This custom is supposed to have originated at a time when heavy fines were imposed for short weights, the additional bread being given by bakers as a precautionary measure.

scenarios.question: A courtier tells Edward VI that Christ's College, a Master and twelve Fellows, is a superstitious number, and to cut a Fellowship or two. What does the king do?
scenarios.answer: Adds a thirteenth Fellowship, to spoil the conceit
wrong: Takes away two Fellowships, as advised
Renames the college after himself
Adds a second Master to make it even
scenarios.note: “Oh, no!” said the King, “I have a better way than that to mar their conceit; I will add a thirteenth Fellowship unto them;” which he did accordingly, and so it remaineth unto this day.

scenarios.question: You're building a house in Siam. What must every staircase have?
scenarios.answer: An uneven number of steps
wrong: A landing every seventh step
Steps facing the rising sun
Twelve steps, one for each month
scenarios.note: every house must have an uneven number of rooms, windows, and doors; each staircase must have an uneven number of steps.

scenarios.question: A Bavarian peasant passing a haunted place carries a new knife marked with three crosses, a loaf baked on Epiphany Eve, and what?
scenarios.answer: A black cat
wrong: A sprig of rowan
A horseshoe
A pinch of salt
scenarios.note: considers himself amply fortified against evil if he takes the precaution to carry three things; namely, (1) a new knife which has never cut anything, marked on the blade with three crosses; (2) a loaf of bread baked on Epiphany Eve; (3) a black cat.

scenarios.question: You're Cato the Censor, told gravely that rats have gnawed your boots. What's your reply?
scenarios.answer: It would portend evil only if the boots had gnawed the rats
wrong: Then the gods want me to stay at home today
Then I shall go to the Senate barefoot
Then send for the soothsayer at once
scenarios.note: “If the boots had gnawed the rats,” he said, “it might have portended evil.”

scenarios.question: You're an ancient Greek farmer with mice in the field. How do you drive them away?
scenarios.answer: Write them a message and stick it on a stone in the field
wrong: Bury a bronze cat at the field's edge
Leave them a share of grain at the gate
Ring a bell at each corner at dawn
scenarios.note: The Grecian husbandmen were accustomed to drive away mice by writing them a message on a piece of paper and sticking it on a stone in the infested field.

scenarios.question: On Christmas Eve, a Bohemian peasant throws the dinner leftovers on the barn floor. What does he say?
scenarios.answer: "O mice, eat these remnants and leave the grain in peace!"
wrong: "Little mice, go to the neighbour's barn!"
"Feast tonight, mice, and fast all year!"
"Christ's Mass for man and mouse alike!"
scenarios.note: whatever food remains from the midday meal is thrown upon the barn floor, and the following sentence is repeated: “O mice, eat these remnants and leave the grain in peace!”

scenarios.question: You're defending some rats summoned to court at Autun. Why can't your clients appear?
scenarios.answer: The road is full of cats, all alert to the case
wrong: The summons wasn't read in their own tongue
It's harvest time and they're busy
Their homes are under the courthouse floor
scenarios.note: He represented to the judge that his clients found it extremely difficult to obey the summons issued to them by the court, owing to their being obliged to traverse a region abounding in cats

scenarios.question: How did people in Britain once believe they could be rid of rats?
scenarios.answer: By cursing them in rhyming verse
wrong: By whistling a tune backwards in the barn
By writing their names on the granary door
By ringing the church bell at midnight
scenarios.note: In Great Britain there formerly prevailed a belief that rats could be rhymed to death by anathematizing them in metrical verse

scenarios.question: Among the Kirghis, you hear a magpie cry from the east. What's coming?
scenarios.answer: Guests
wrong: A journey
Something remarkable
Something evil
scenarios.note: If from the north, it portends evil; from the south, a remarkable occurrence; from the east, it denotes the coming of guests; and from the west, a journey.

scenarios.question: Why, say the Bohemians, does a great horse let a little child lead it?
scenarios.answer: It sees everything ten times bigger than it is
wrong: It knows children can see spirits
It remembers being a foal itself
Children smell of milk, which calms it
scenarios.note: It is a Bohemian superstition that a horse sees everything magnified tenfold, and that this is the reason why the noble animal submits to being led by a little child.
